questions.question: You just installed Git. Which command sets the name recorded on **every** commit you make on this computer?
questions.explanation: `--global` writes to your user config (`~/.gitconfig`), which applies to every repository. Without `--global`, `git config` writes to `.git/config` of the current repository only. Set `user.email` the same way: `git config --global user.email ada@example.com`.

questions.question: `user.email` is set in the system config, your global config, and the repository's own `.git/config`. Which value does a commit in that repository use?
options: Git stops with an error about conflicting settings
questions.explanation: Git reads system → global → local, and the most specific one wins. That makes it easy to use a work email in one repository: run `git config user.email ada@work.com` inside it, without `--global`.

questions.question: A setting behaves unexpectedly and you want to know which config file it comes from. Which command shows every setting together with its file?
questions.explanation: `--show-origin` prints the file before each setting. To look at one key, use `git config --show-origin user.email`. `git config --global --edit` opens only the global file in your editor.

questions.question: You have a project folder on disk that isn't under version control yet. How do you turn it into a Git repository?
options: Run `git add .` inside the folder; Git creates the repository automatically
Run `git remote add origin` inside the folder
questions.explanation: `git init` creates the hidden `.git` folder, which *is* the repository: all history, branches and config live there. Your files are untouched; nothing is tracked until you `git add` and `git commit`. `git clone` is for copying an existing repository.

questions.question: What does this command give you?
options: A folder `webshop` with the full history, a remote called `origin`, and the default branch checked out
A folder `shop` with only the latest version of the files
A folder `webshop` with the files but no `.git` folder
A new empty repository on GitHub called `webshop`
questions.explanation: The last argument names the target folder; without it Git uses `shop`. A clone copies every commit, sets up `origin` pointing at the URL, creates remote-tracking branches such as `origin/main`, and checks out the default branch.

questions.question: A repository has 15 years of history and you only need the latest files, for a CI build. Which command downloads the least?
questions.explanation: `--depth 1` makes a **shallow clone** with only the most recent commit. `--single-branch` still downloads the full history of that one branch. `--bare` gets everything but without a working tree, which is what servers use.

questions.question: `git init` keeps creating a branch called `master`, but your team uses `main`. How do you change that for every new repository?
questions.explanation: `init.defaultBranch` sets the name of the first branch in new repositories. `git branch -m master main` renames the branch in the current repository only, which is the fix for one that already exists.

questions.question: Which line in `.gitignore` ignores every `.log` file, in any folder of the project?
questions.explanation: A pattern without a slash matches in every folder. A leading slash anchors it to the folder of the `.gitignore` file, so `/*.log` only ignores logs in the root. A trailing slash (`build/`) matches folders only. A `!` in front re-includes a file: `!keep.log`.

questions.question: You added `config.env` to `.gitignore`, but `git status` still shows it as modified. It was committed last week. How do you stop tracking it but keep the file on disk?
options: Nothing: Git picks up the `.gitignore` change after the next commit
questions.explanation:
`.gitignore` only applies to **untracked** files. A file that is already tracked stays tracked until you remove it from the index. `--cached` removes it from the index only, so the file stays on disk. Without `--cached`, `git rm` deletes the file too.

If the file holds a secret, it is still in the old commits: rotate the secret.

questions.question: A new file doesn't show up in `git status` and you suspect a `.gitignore` rule somewhere. Which command tells you which rule, in which file, ignores it?
questions.explanation: `git check-ignore -v` prints the file, line number and pattern that match, which is handy when rules come from nested `.gitignore` files or a global excludes file. `git status --ignored` lists ignored files but doesn't say why.

questions.question: You want to type `git st` instead of `git status`. Which command sets that up?
questions.explanation: Aliases live in config under `alias.<name>`. A popular one is `git config --global alias.lg 'log --oneline --graph --all'`. An alias that starts with `!` runs a shell command.

questions.question: What's the quickest way to see the options of `git commit` as a short summary in the terminal?
questions.explanation: `-h` prints a compact usage summary for any subcommand. `git help commit` (or `git commit --help`) opens the full manual page, which is the place to go for the details.

questions.question: `git commit` without `-m` opens Vim, and you'd rather write messages in VS Code. Which setting do you need?
questions.explanation: `core.editor` picks the editor for commit messages, interactive rebases and tags. `--wait` matters: without it VS Code returns immediately, and Git sees an empty message and aborts the commit.

questions.question: Windows and macOS teammates keep producing diffs where every line changed, only because of CRLF versus LF line endings. What is the most robust fix for the whole team?
options: Ask everyone to run `git config core.ignorecase true`
questions.explanation: `.gitattributes` is committed, so the rule applies to everyone. `* text=auto` lets Git store LF in the repository and convert on checkout as needed. The per-person alternative is `core.autocrlf` (`true` on Windows, `input` on macOS and Linux), but that depends on everyone setting it.
